\begin{abstract}
Whether a medical vision-language model (VLM) uses the image is commonly assessed by removing the image: the
consistent-but-dangerous taxonomy labels an answer \dang{} when it is stable under paraphrase and unchanged
without the image. We ask whether this criterion supports comparisons between models. Three medical VLMs and
the general-purpose models they were derived from (MedGemma-4B and MedGemma-1.5-4B \vs Gemma-3-4B;
MedVLThinker-3B \vs Qwen2.5-VL-3B) answer 3,365 questions on 907 CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology images, both
without the image and under three \emph{in-format} probes that keep an image in the input: a different image, a
black image, and an image for which the same question has the opposite answer. The analysis was pre-registered,
and each subsequent probe and model pair was registered before it was run. Under image removal, MedGemma-4B has
a 13.7-point\ci{10.0}{17.5} higher \dang{} share than Gemma-3-4B. No in-format probe corroborates this: of the
nine model-pair~$\times$~dataset comparisons, image removal separates the two models in five, and in none of these
does an in-format probe agree. The image-removal differences instead track refusal (without an image, Gemma-3
declines on 29\% of questions, and its forced answers there are unrelated to its answers with the image) and the
agreement between a model's priors and the image. In-format probes have their own confound: both MedGemma models
follow opposite-answer images far more than Gemma-3 on SLAKE, which they were trained on (+48.0 and +36.5
points), but not on held-out PathVQA (+0.8 and $-5.6$). We conclude that image removal does not measure image
reliance, and that comparisons of image reliance require in-format probes on data outside each model's training
set.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not performing visual question
answering, however accurate its answers. In general-domain VQA, this concern motivated balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still evaluated predominantly by
accuracy, although the stakes are higher: an answer derived from language priors is most likely to fail on
exactly the patients whose images are atypical.

Neither accuracy nor consistency under rephrasing distinguishes using the image from guessing well; a model that
ignores the image can be \emph{more} consistent, since no visual signal perturbs it~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed}.
Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore combined the two criteria per answer. An
answer is \emph{consistent} if it is stable under paraphrase, and \emph{image-reliant} if it changes when the
image is removed. The resulting quadrants are \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent, not reliant) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays, they found that fine-tuning for
consistency moves most answers into \dang{}.

Such a taxonomy invites comparisons between models, and these comparisons are only as valid as the reliance
criterion. Removing the image changes the input format: a model asked about an absent image may decline, answer
from priors, or guess, and none of these responses is equivalent to ignoring an image that is present. We
therefore compare image removal with probes that keep an image in the input, on the same questions, for three
medical VLMs and the general-purpose models they were derived from: MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} and
MedGemma-1.5-4B against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, and MedVLThinker-3B against Qwen2.5-VL-3B, on CT,
MRI, X-ray and pathology questions from three public benchmarks.

\Cref{fig:bydataset} summarizes the results. Image removal reports differences between medical and general models
that no in-format probe corroborates, in every model pair and dataset where it reports a difference. Conversely,
the in-format probes indicate substantially greater image reliance for both MedGemma models only on SLAKE, a
dataset in their training data; on PathVQA, which none of the medical models was trained on, a pre-registered test
finds no such advantage.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item A comparison of four reliance probes on identical questions for three medical/general model pairs and three
datasets, showing that between-model differences under image removal are not corroborated by any in-format probe.
The individual probes have precedent~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent,zafar2026see,lotfinia2026cxr}; to our
knowledge, their conclusions about the same models have not been compared.
\item Evidence for two mechanisms behind the image-removal differences: refusal under a forced yes/no format, and
agreement between a model's prior and the image content.
\item A pre-registered held-out test showing that the in-format advantage of two medical models on their
training distribution does not transfer, so that in-format probes also require held-out data.
\item Two corrections to the \dang{} share: its chance floor on yes/no questions, addressed with Cohen's $\kappa$,
and a paired decomposition into correct and incorrect \dang{} answers.
\item An open, pre-registered pipeline covering three datasets, four modalities and five models, including a
paraphrase set screened pair by pair for equivalence and the observation that bf16 batching perturbs
log-probabilities by up to 1~nat.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors in VQA.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors; text-only baselines are the
corresponding control in medical VQA.

\paragraph{Image use in medical VLMs.} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates across
medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates frequently co-occur with high text-only agreement. The
quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} defines reliance by image removal and corroborates it with a
KL-divergence score, a black image and random image swaps, which agreed with image removal on their models.
Zafar~\etal~\cite{zafar2026see} construct blank, pixel-shuffled, absent and CLIP-retrieved hard-negative images
to define reliance metrics and train a model against them. Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} swap and
occlude chest radiographs and find that model class (medical or general) does not predict image use. Pathology
VLMs reach high accuracy without the image~\cite{zhang2026pathology}, and medical MLLMs frequently attend to
irrelevant regions~\cite{liu2026medmllmfail}. Grounding inputs can even reduce closed-ended
accuracy~\cite{chen2026grounding}; HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} and MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval}
benchmark localization and hallucination. These studies use a single probe or treat several as interchangeable;
we compare the conclusions of different probes about the same models, inside and outside the models' training
data.

\paragraph{Answering without evidence.} MedVIGIL~\cite{jiang2026medvigil} tests whether models abstain when
visual evidence is corrupted, and Vohra~\cite{vohra2026hearsay} reports that frontier VLMs produce diagnoses for
images that were never provided. Four of our five open models decline almost always when permitted to; we show how
enforcing an answer affects a reliance criterion.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest-ranked ones is evaluated
by AUROC and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use this framework to test whether image reliance
identifies errors.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 test and validation questions; the only
dataset with modality labels, with the validation split included so that each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions from the original
release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600 yes/no and 200
open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). A question is yes/no if its reference answer is \emph{yes} or
\emph{no}. The \textbf{primary analysis set} comprises the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670 images.
Probe R4 uses a separate set: all 1,192 PathVQA test and validation yes/no questions that are also asked of another
image with the opposite answer (682 images). Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed in committed
manifests, so that every run receives identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-based
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data. Its technical
report~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} lists SLAKE (450 items, the size of SLAKE's training split) and VQA-RAD
(reinforcement-learning stage) among its training data and states that PathVQA was excluded.
\textbf{Gemma-3-4B} (\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) has the same architecture and size. \textbf{MedGemma-1.5-4B}
(\texttt{google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it}, released in 2026; its model card lists SLAKE) is compared with the same
Gemma-3-4B, and \textbf{MedVLThinker-3B} (\texttt{UCSC-VLAA/MedVLThinker-3B-RL\_PMC}, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct
trained with reinforcement learning on PMC-VQA) with its base model \textbf{Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct}. A medical
model and its base differ in their entire post-training, not only in medical data; we therefore compare
\emph{checkpoints} rather than attribute differences to medical training as such. All five models run unquantized
in bf16 on a single 16\,GB GPU, since quantization would perturb the probabilities under study, and receive
identical prompts: a fixed system message, the question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.'' or ``Answer with
a single word or short phrase.'' Each model added after the primary pair passed a registered format check
(mean first-token yes/no probability mass with the image $\ge0.9$ in every dataset of a 330-question pilot;
observed 0.93--0.999).

\subsection{Probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Each question is posed with its own image (\textbf{orig}) and as screened paraphrases with the same image
(\textbf{para$_k$}; \cref{sec:para}). Image reliance is probed by altering only the image or the instruction:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Image removed} (\emph{noimg}): image tokens omitted, text unchanged; the reliance criterion of the
taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}.
\item \textbf{Wrong image} (\emph{shuf}): another image from the same dataset and modality, selected by a hash of
the question identifier.
\item \textbf{R1, black image}: a black image in place of the original, preserving the input format but removing
the content.
\item \textbf{R2, abstention permitted}: image removed, with the instruction extended by ``If this cannot be
determined without seeing the image, answer `unknown'.''
\item \textbf{R3, opposite-answer image}: another image of the same dataset and modality for which the
\emph{same} question has the opposite reference answer; a model that uses the image must change its answer.
Partners exist for 367 SLAKE yes/no questions (130 images), whose templated questions recur across images.
\item \textbf{R4}: R3 applied to the 1,192 PathVQA questions above, outside the listed training data of every
medical model.
\end{itemize}
We refer to the wrong-image, black-image and opposite-answer probes as \emph{in-format} probes, since an image is
present in the input. The first two probes belong to the pre-registered main run; R1--R4 and the two additional
model pairs were each registered after the results that motivated them and before they were run.

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} are obtained from a single forward pass,
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$, over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is recorded as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} are decoded greedily and scored by token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with a guard that
prevents opposite terms (left/right, upper/lower, \etc) from matching. An answer is \textbf{consistent} if the
answers to the first two valid paraphrases equal the \emph{orig} answer, and \textbf{reliant} under a probe if the
probe answer differs from the \emph{orig} answer; the share of reliant answers is the \textbf{answer-change rate}
of that probe. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from (consistent, reliant). \textbf{Refusal} is $m<0.5$, \ie the
majority of first-token mass falls on neither \emph{yes} nor \emph{no}; free generation confirms that these
responses are requests for the image (\cref{fig:teaser}a). \textbf{Pair accuracy} (R3, R4) is the share of swaps
answered correctly on both images, which is zero by construction for a model that ignores the image. The
\textbf{image PMI} of an answer $\hat y$ is $\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat y\mid\varnothing,q)$.
\textbf{Chance correction} uses Cohen's $\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and probe answers; the
\emph{chance floor} of the \dang{} share is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$, where $p_e$ is the agreement expected
from the two answer distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates are
generated by Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy decoding; five styles) and by two deterministic
templates that copy every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X present?''). A rule-based validator rejects
changes to laterality, negation and absence terms, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer
leakage, near-copies and length. Two audit rounds accepted 81\% and 83\% of sampled pairs, below the pre-specified
85\%; we therefore tightened the rules, excluded a ``plain language'' style, and \textbf{judged every unique
rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair}, 4,890 in total, against a written rubric (\cref{app:rubric}). The judge
was an LLM (Claude); see \cref{sec:limits}. It rejected 1,208 pairs, each with a recorded reason (\eg
\emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}); unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. Of
the primary-set questions, 84\% retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use these (1,012
questions, 600 images).

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were fixed before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every later
change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are identified as such. Because several questions share
an image, all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$), with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Holm correction~\cite{holm1979} is applied within four families
(\cref{tab:tests}): \textbf{P1a--c} (accuracy without the image minus the majority-answer prior) and \textbf{P2}
(AUROC of image PMI minus AUROC of confidence); \textbf{H6--H8} (probes R1--R3, MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3);
\textbf{H9--H11} (additional pairs, medical $-$ general: more frequent following of R3 images, fewer answer changes
without the image, less refusal); and \textbf{H12a--c} (R4, with a decision rule fixed in advance). \textbf{P3},
the paired difference in \dang{} share, forms a separate family. A finding is considered robust only if its sign
holds across a grid of F1 thresholds (0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and ``strong'' flips.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
All runs completed: 18,896 model calls per model in the main run, 3,535 for R1--R3 and 2,384 for R4, for each of
the five models. The pipeline reproduces MedGemma's published SLAKE score (token-F1 70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3
on the model card; Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs 40.2), and the yes/no format mass with the image is $\ge0.997$ in every
dataset. With the image, MedGemma-4B is more accurate than Gemma-3 on yes/no questions by 18 points on SLAKE and
25 on VQA-RAD, both part of its training data, and by 2 points on PathVQA, which is not (\cref{tab:acc}).

\subsection{Under image removal, the medical models appear less image-reliant}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.pdf}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test split), MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3-4B. Left: reliance assessed
by removing the image (the taxonomy's definition). Right: by a different image of the same modality. Shares are
uncorrected; on yes/no questions they include chance agreement (\cref{sec:chance}) and correct answers
(\cref{sec:what}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

Under image removal, MedGemma-4B's \dang{} share is 50.6/46.8/56.5\% (PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD), compared with
43.2/28.1/31.0\% for Gemma-3 (\cref{fig:quad}, left). The paired difference, \textbf{P3 $=+13.7$
points}\ci{10.0}{17.5} ($p<0.001$; 1,012 questions, 600 images), is positive in every dataset (PathVQA
+7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9}, VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}) and in every cell of the
sensitivity grid. MedGemma-4B is also the more consistent model (paraphrase flip rate 6.8\% \vs 13.6\% on SLAKE),
and MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern (+9.8\ci{5.8}{13.9}). Taken at face value, the medical models more often
give stable, confident answers that do not depend on the image.

\subsection{No in-format probe corroborates image removal}
\label{sec:disagree}
\Cref{fig:bydataset} reports the answer-change rate of every probe by model pair and dataset. Image removal
separates the medical model from its base in five of the nine cells: lower change rates for both MedGemma models
on VQA-RAD ($-19.1$\ci{$-27.6$}{$-10.4$} and $-18.7$\ci{$-27.3$}{$-9.4$}) and for MedGemma-4B on SLAKE
($-9.9$\ci{$-14.9$}{$-4.4$}), and higher rates for MedVLThinker on PathVQA and VQA-RAD (+4.5\ci{1.7}{7.2} and
+11.2\ci{5.3}{17.4}). In four of these cells, no in-format probe detects a difference, and their intervals
exclude a difference as large as the one image removal reports; in the fifth, MedGemma-4B on SLAKE, every in-format probe shows a
difference in the opposite direction (wrong image +11.8, black image +33.0, opposite-answer image +48.0 points).
Pooled over datasets, the primary pair shows the same divergence: image removal $-6.1$\ci{$-9.5$}{$-2.7$}, wrong
image +5.1\ci{1.7}{8.5}, black image +20.3\ci{15.9}{24.6}. The two main-run probes also agree poorly at the
question level ($\kappa$ between their reliance labels: $-0.11$ to 0.23), and the modality ordering of the \dang{}
share reverses between them, partly because a randomly chosen partner image often has the same correct answer
(all 23 chest X-ray partners that pose the same question).

\paragraph{In-format probes on SLAKE.} The registered probes R1 and R3 were run on the primary pair after the main
results. H6, which predicted that MedGemma-4B's answers would be more stable under a black image, was not
supported; the effect was in the opposite direction ($\kappa(\text{image},\text{black})=0.11$ \vs 0.33). On a
black image, MedGemma-4B's yes-rate falls from 58\% to 28\%, consistent with reading an empty image as an absence
of findings, whereas Gemma-3's rises from 64\% to 84\%. H8 was supported: on SLAKE's opposite-answer swaps,
MedGemma-4B follows the image in 72.8\% of cases and Gemma-3 in 24.8\%, and MedGemma-4B answers both images
correctly in 71.7\% of swaps, compared with 23.4\%. MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern on SLAKE (H9,
+36.5\ci{30.6}{42.1}); MedVLThinker does not differ from its base under any in-format probe on any dataset, apart
from a small black-image difference on SLAKE ($-3.4$\ci{$-6.5$}{$-0.3$}). \Cref{sec:r4} tests whether the MedGemma
advantage extends beyond SLAKE.

\subsection{Sources of the image-removal differences}
\label{sec:what}
\paragraph{Refusal.} The pre-registered format check ($m\ge0.9$) failed in a single condition, image removal. Free
generation shows why: ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image to determine if there is a
spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3). Without the image, Gemma-3 declines on 354 of the 1,206 questions, MedGemma-4B on
219 and MedGemma-1.5 on 8 (\cref{fig:abst}); MedVLThinker and Qwen2.5-VL never decline. On declined questions, the
forced answer is predominantly \emph{no} and unrelated to the model's answer with the image ($\kappa=-0.01$ for
Gemma-3, 0.04 for MedGemma-4B), so 53--55\% of these answers are classified as image-reliant. The largest
image-removal differences occur where refusal rates differ most: on VQA-RAD, Gemma-3 declines on half of the
questions, 23 points more often than MedGemma-4B and 48 points more often than MedGemma-1.5. When abstention is
permitted (R2), MedGemma-4B declines on 93.0\% of questions and Gemma-3 on 99.7\% (H7, $-6.7$), eliminating most of
the 11.2-point difference observed under the forced format. For MedGemma-1.5, which almost never declines, the
\dang{} difference falls to +3.0\ci{$-3.6$}{9.5} on the 467 questions that both models answer.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.pdf}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model declines to answer when the image is removed ($m<0.5$;
95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images). Top: the main-run instruction (``Answer with only yes or no''). Bottom:
probe R2, whose instruction permits ``unknown''.}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Agreement between prior and image.} Refusal does not account for all of the difference: on the 436
questions that both MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3 answer without the image ($m\ge0.9$), P3 remains +8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3},
and image removal still separates the two Qwen-based models, neither of which declines. When a model's prior
matches the image content, its answer is the same with and without the image, and image removal classifies the
answer as image-independent. MedGemma-4B's answers without the image exceed the majority-answer prior on PathVQA,
which it was not trained on (P1a, +5.0; +11.9\ci{7.1}{16.6} among questions it answers), and agree with its
answers with the image beyond chance ($\kappa=0.21$ \vs 0.11 for Gemma-3). In the Qwen pair, the base model's
answers without the image agree more ($\kappa=0.16$ \vs 0.09), and image removal correspondingly classifies the base
model as less reliant. The correctness decomposition shows the composition of MedGemma-4B's excess (\cref{fig:p3},
bottom): \dang{}-and-correct is 39.2\% \vs 25.1\% (+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}), whereas \dang{}-and-incorrect, the
category that would mislead a user, is 11.3\% \vs 11.7\% ($-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0}). MedGemma-1.5's excess is
likewise correct (+9.3 correct, +0.5 incorrect).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_p3.pdf}
\caption{MedGemma-4B $-$ Gemma-3 difference in \dang{} share under each probe and subset, and decomposed by whether
the \dang{} answer is correct (paired; 95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images).}
\label{fig:p3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Held-out data (probe R4)}
\label{sec:r4}
Both MedGemma models were trained on SLAKE (the evaluated images are disjoint from its training split, but the
image distribution and question templates are shared), whereas MedVLThinker was not. Training exposure therefore
explains the SLAKE results as well as greater image reliance does. R4 repeats the opposite-answer probe for all
five models on PathVQA, which was excluded from MedGemma's training (\cref{tab:tests}). Every model follows the
partner image in 43--49\% of the 1,192 swaps and answers both images correctly in 36--43\%, far above the 0\% of a
model that ignores the image: all five models use pathology images, to a similar degree. MedGemma-4B does not differ
from Gemma-3 (H12a: +0.8\ci{$-2.7$}{4.2}), MedGemma-1.5 follows the image \emph{less} often (H12b:
$-5.6$\ci{$-9.1$}{$-2.0$}, $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.003$), and MedVLThinker matches its base as predicted (H12c).
Resampling PathVQA's 154 question templates instead of images leads to the same conclusions. Under the decision rule
fixed before the run, the SLAKE difference is attributed to the training distribution, and the hypothesis that
either MedGemma model relies on the image more than Gemma-3 is withdrawn. Accuracy shows the same pattern:
MedGemma-4B's advantage over Gemma-3 is 18 points on SLAKE yes/no questions and 2 points on PathVQA
(\cref{tab:acc}). On PathVQA, only the black-image probe separates MedGemma-4B from Gemma-3 (+19.2), consistent with
its response to an empty image rather than with greater use of image content; the content-based probes (different
image, opposite-answer image) show no difference.

\subsection{The chance floor}
\label{sec:chance}
An answer is classified as image-independent whenever the answer without the image equals the answer with it,
which on yes/no questions frequently occurs by chance. On the P3 set, MedGemma-4B's answers are unchanged without
the image in 58.6\% of cases, against 49.1\% expected from its answer distributions alone (Gemma-3: 49.7\% \vs
45.7\%). Combined with consistency, this yields a \textbf{chance floor of 41.5\% (MedGemma-4B) and 35.8\%
(Gemma-3)}, against observed \dang{} shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%. Approximately 6 of the 13.7 points of P3 reflect
the difference in floors, partly because MedGemma-4B is more consistent (84.5\% \vs 78.4\%), a desirable property
that the metric counts against it. The chance-corrected difference is $\Delta\kappa=+0.112$\ci{0.044}{0.180}.

\subsection{Image reliance does not identify errors}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.pdf}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test split, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as an error signal. Ranking
yes/no answers by image PMI separates correct from incorrect answers at chance level (\cref{fig:sel}; AUROC
\textbf{0.513}\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma-4B, 0.532 for Gemma-3), whereas the model's own confidence reaches
0.709 and 0.603 (P2: higher by 0.197\ci{0.145}{0.250} and 0.071\ci{0.026}{0.116}). The degree to which an answer
depends on the image is thus not informative about its correctness.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{What image removal measures.} Removing the image poses a question about an image that is absent. The
response depends first on whether the model answers at all and on the quality of its priors, and only then on
whether it would have used the image. Across three model pairs and three datasets, every difference that image
removal reported between a medical model and its base was uncorroborated by the in-format probes, and the largest
differences coincided with the largest differences in refusal. The corroborating checks of the original study
(black image, random swaps) agreed with image removal on its chest X-ray models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent};
on our models and data they do not. A \dang{} share is therefore underspecified without its probe, and a
comparison of \dang{} shares obtained by image removal may reflect refusal policy more than image use.

\paragraph{What the in-format probes measure.} The in-format probes are not free of confounds either. On SLAKE,
they indicate that both MedGemma models rely on the image far more than Gemma-3; on PathVQA, outside their training
data, they do not. Image reliance is a property of a model \emph{and} a data distribution, and in-format probes
evaluated on a model's training distribution may reflect what the model learned there rather than how it uses
images in general. For the three pairs studied, no general claim of greater image reliance by the medical model
survives evaluation on held-out data.

\paragraph{Residual risk.} MedGemma-4B's additional \dang{} answers are correct, and the share of stable,
image-independent and incorrect answers is the same for both models. MedGemma-4B makes fewer errors overall (25.7\%
\vs 37.6\%), but a larger share of them fall into this category (44\% \vs 31\%, +12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}); such errors
would not be detected by consistency or reliance checks.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Assess reliance with in-format probes, preferably with an
image that requires a different answer, and report the agreement between probes. (2)~Evaluate in-format probes on
data outside each model's training set, and consult training documentation before comparing models. (3)~Report the
\dang{} share together with its chance floor, or as $\kappa$; on balanced yes/no data, a model whose answers
without the image are pure noise is about 50\% ``not reliant''. (4)~Decompose \dang{} answers by correctness.
(5)~Permit abstention, and treat declining without an image as appropriate behavior rather than as a format
failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
Three model pairs from two families establish that image removal \emph{can} disagree with in-format probes and
indicate why; they do not establish how often this occurs across models. The refusal and prior-agreement accounts
and the per-dataset analysis (\cref{fig:bydataset}) were formulated after the primary results; among the
dataset-specific comparisons, only R4 was registered. R4 covers a single modality, pathology, on which all models
perform modestly (pair accuracy 36--43\%); it argues against a general advantage but cannot exclude one in every
domain. R3 and the SLAKE results rest on templated questions that recur across images; resampling templates instead
of images leaves the conclusions unchanged. MedGemma-4B was also trained on VQA-RAD, nearly all of whose test images
appear in its training split, so its VQA-RAD results may reflect exposure; the training data of the general models
are not published. A medical model and its base differ in their entire post-training, not only in medical data.
Refusal is inferred from first-token probability mass and confirmed on a sample by free generation. Paraphrase
equivalence was judged by an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by independent human raters}; a check of 50
paraphrases, rated by the author with AI assistance, accepted 88\% (above the pre-specified 85\%) but is not
independent of AI judgment. This is the principal limitation of the consistency measure; the probe comparison does
not use paraphrases. PathVQA questions are generated automatically and are often ungrammatical. The chance
correction and the correctness and refusal decompositions were introduced after the results were known. Excluding
the 330 pilot questions used to tune the design leaves every conclusion unchanged (P1a +6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}, P3
+12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}). Benchmark VQA is not clinical use, and we make no clinical claims.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
By the image-removal criterion, MedGemma-4B gives image-independent answers more often than its general-purpose
counterpart. No probe that keeps an image in the input corroborates this difference, in any model pair or dataset
we examined. Image removal measures whether a model answers without an image and whether its priors agree with the
image, rather than how much it relies on the image; probes that keep the image indicate greater reliance for the
medical models only on data they were trained on. Comparisons of image reliance between models therefore require
in-format probes on held-out data, together with chance correction and a decomposition by correctness.

\appendix
\section{Implementation details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} The experiments are implemented as a Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line
interface: \texttt{prepare} (download, deterministic sampling, hash-verified images), \texttt{paraphrase}
(generation with rule-based and judgment-based validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in
parts with checkpoint analysis), \texttt{probes} (R1--R3), \texttt{contrast} (R4), and \texttt{analyze},
\texttt{compare}, \texttt{posthoc}, \texttt{replication} and \texttt{contamination}, which produce all tables and
figures in this paper. Configurations are layered by base, profile, model and hardware. Each job is a (question,
condition) pair keyed by identifier, so that interrupted runs resume without recomputation; every run records its
configuration, commit and library versions. Registrations are git tags.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19, bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080 SUPER
(16\,GB). MedGemma-4B requires 0.23\,s per call (18,896 calls in about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak memory). During
pre-flight testing, we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} alone changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up
to 1.09 nats (median 0.17) on identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most 0.008. An fp32
output head did not remove the effect, which therefore originates inside the network. All runs consequently use
batch size 1, at a cost of about 1.5$\times$ in throughput. A regression check reproduced the pilot run, performed
on a T4, on the final GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean $|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 103 unit tests and 7 tests with real models cover, among others, scoring edge cases, the
paraphrase rules (including every failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resumption,
the coverage of the cluster bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, the chance correction of
$\kappa$, the construction of opposite-answer partners, and an oracle-\vs-blind check of pair accuracy.

\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if both questions ask exactly the same thing, so that the correct answer cannot
differ. Permitted: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), and reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
statement of fact turned into one of possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be
enlarged?''); a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract,
skull fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modalities (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or altered relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass lateral
to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy, coronal$\to$transverse); two
questions in one; and malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364, modality of statement 106,
added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus rejections of the
template-based pass).
